title: De Divinatione
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
source: Translated by Claude from phi0474.phi053.perseus-lat2, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Perseus Digital Library and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: magnifica quaedam res et salutaris, si modo est ulla, quaque proxime ad deorum vim natura mortalis possit accedere. itaque ut alia nos melius multa quam Graeci, sic huic praestantissimae rei nomen nostri a divis, Graeci, ut Plato interpretatur, a furore duxerunt.
passages.english: [It is] a splendid and salutary thing, if only there is any such thing, and one by which mortal nature could come closest to the power of the gods. And so, just as we [Romans] have done many other things better than the Greeks, so our ancestors derived the name of this most excellent thing from the gods (*divi*), whereas the Greeks, as Plato explains, derived it from madness.
passages.notes: The wordplay is divinatio from divi; the Greek mantikē is linked by Plato to mania (madness).

passages.original: An medicine ars non putanda est? quam tamen multa fallunt. quid? gubernatores nonne falluntur? An Achivorum exercitus et tot navium rectores non ita profecti sunt ab Ilio, ut 'profectione laeti piscium lasciviam intuerentur,' ut ait Pacuvius, ' nec tuendi satietas capere posset?' interea prope iam óccidente sóle inhorrescít mare,ténebrae conduplicántur noctisque ét nimbum occaecát nigror. Num igitur tot clarissimorum ducum regumque naufragium sustulit artem gubernandi?
passages.english:
Is medicine not to be thought an art? Yet many things deceive it. What then? Are pilots not deceived? Did not the army of the Achaeans and the captains of so many ships set out from Ilium in such a way that, "glad at their departure, they watched the sporting of the fish," as Pacuvius says, "and could not have their fill of watching"?
Meanwhile, with the sun now almost setting, the sea grows rough,
the darkness doubles, and the blackness of night and storm-cloud blinds [them].
Did the shipwreck of so many most illustrious leaders and kings, then, abolish the art of piloting?

passages.original: carent autem arte ei qui, non ratione aut coniectura observatis ac notatis signis, sed concitatione quadam animi aut soluto liberoque motu, futura praesentiunt, quod et somniantibus saepe contingit et non numquam vaticinantibus per furorem, ut Bacis Boeotius, ut Epimenides Cres, ut Sibylla Erythraea. cuius generis oracula etiam habenda sunt, non ea, quae aequatis sortibus ducuntur, sed illa, quae instinctu divino afflatuque funduntur; etsi ipsa sors contemnenda non est, si auctoritatem habet vetustatis, ut eae sunt sortes, quas e terra editas accepimus;
passages.english: Those, on the other hand, lack art who foresee the future not by reason or conjecture from signs observed and recorded, but by a certain excitement of the mind, or by a free and unfettered movement [of it]. This often happens to people when they dream, and sometimes to those who prophesy in a frenzy, like Bacis the Boeotian, like Epimenides the Cretan, like the Erythraean Sibyl. To this class must also be assigned oracles: not those that are drawn by lots evenly shaken, but those that are poured forth by divine impulse and inspiration. And yet the lot itself is not to be despised, if it has the authority of antiquity, as do those lots which, we are told, sprang from the earth;

passages.original: Num te ad fabulas revoco vel nostrorum vel Graecorum poëtarum? narrat enim et apud Ennium Vestalis illa: excita cum tremulis anus attulit artubu' lumen,talia tum memorat lacrimans exterrita somno:' Eurydica prognata, pater quam noster amavit,vires vitaque corpu' meum nunc deserit omne.nam me visus homo pulcher per amoena salicta et ripas raptare locosque novos;
passages.english:
Am I calling you back to the tales of the poets, whether ours or the Greeks'? For in Ennius too that Vestal tells [her dream]:
When the old woman, roused, had brought a light with trembling limbs,
then, weeping, terrified out of sleep, she tells these things:
"Daughter of Eurydice, whom our father loved,
strength and life are now deserting my whole body.
For a handsome man seemed to carry me off through pleasant willow-groves
and riverbanks and strange places;
passages.notes: The Vestal is Ilia, mother of Romulus and Remus; the line breaks off mid-sentence.

passages.original: Sed propiora videamus. cuiusnam modi est Superbi Tarquini somnium, de quo in Bruto Acci loquitur ipse?
passages.english: But let us look at nearer things. Of what kind is the dream of Tarquin the Proud, of which he himself speaks in the Brutus of Accius?

passages.original: Est apud Platonem Socrates, cum esset in custodia publica, dicens Critoni, suo familiari, sibi post tertium diem esse moriendum; vidisse enim se in somnis pulchritudine eximia feminam, quae se nomine appellans, diceret Homericum quendam eius modi versum: tertia te Phthiae tempestas laeta locabit.quod, ut est dictum, sic scribitur contigisse.
passages.english:
In Plato there is Socrates, when he was in the public prison, telling Crito, his friend, that he would have to die after the third day; for he had seen in his sleep a woman of exceptional beauty who, calling him by name, spoke a Homeric verse of this kind:
The third fair day will set you in Phthia.
And it is written that this happened just as it had been said.

passages.original: ei visum in quiete egregia facie iuvenem dicere fore ut perbrevi convalesceret, paucisque diebus interiturum Alexandrum tyrannum, ipsum autem Eudemum quinquennio post domum esse rediturum. atque ita quidem prima statim scribit Aristoteles consecuta, et convaluisse Eudemum, et ab uxoris fratribus interfectum tyrannum; quinto autem anno exeunte, cum esset spes ex illo somnio in Cyprum ilium ex Sicilia esse rediturum, proeliantem eum ad Syracusas occidisse;
passages.english: [He wrote that] in his sleep Eudemus saw a young man of outstanding beauty, who told him that he would very soon recover, that the tyrant Alexander would perish within a few days, and that Eudemus himself would return home five years later. And indeed, Aristotle writes, the first [predictions] were fulfilled at once: Eudemus recovered, and the tyrant was killed by his wife's brothers. But at the end of the fifth year, when on the strength of that dream there was hope that he would return from Sicily to Cyprus, he fell fighting near Syracuse;

passages.original: Marium cum fascibus laureatis quaerere ex te, quid tristis esses, cumque tu te patria vi pulsum esse dixisses, prehendisse eum dextram tuam et bono animo te iussisse esse lictorique proximo tradidisse, ut te in monumentum suum deduceret, et dixisse in eo tibi salutem fore. tum et se exclamasse Sallustius narrat reditum tibi celerem et gloriosum paratum, et te ipsum visum somnio delectari. nam illud mihi ipsi celeriter nuntiatum est ut audivisses in monumento Mari de tuo reditu magnificentissimum illud senatus consultum esse factum referente optimo et clarissimo viro consule, idque frequentissimo theatro incredibili clamore et plausu comprobatum, dixisse te nihil illo Atinati somnio fieri posse divinius.
passages.english: [you dreamed that] Gaius Marius, with his fasces wreathed in laurel, asked you why you were sad, and when you said that you had been driven from your country by violence, he took your right hand, told you to be of good heart, and handed you over to the nearest lictor to escort you to his monument, saying that there you would find safety. Then, Sallustius relates, he himself exclaimed that a swift and glorious return awaited you, and you yourself seemed delighted by the dream. For it was reported to me myself soon afterwards that, when you heard that it was in the monument of Marius that the magnificent decree of the senate about your return had been passed, on the motion of the excellent and most distinguished consul, and that it had been approved in a packed theatre with incredible shouting and applause, you said that nothing could be more divine than that dream at Atina.
passages.notes: The 'C.' (Gaius) at the end of the preceding context belongs to Marius here. The monument of Marius was a temple of Honos and Virtus where the senate met.

passages.original: Divinare autem morientes illo etiam exemplo confirmat Posidonius, quod affert, Rhodium quendam morientem sex aequales nominasse et dixisse, qui primus eorum, qui secundus, qui deinde deinceps moriturus esset. sed tribus modis censet deorum appulsu homines somniare: uno, quod praevideat animus ipse per sese, quippe qui deorum cognatione teneatur;
passages.english: Posidonius also confirms that the dying divine by this example, which he adduces: that a certain Rhodian, when dying, named six men of his own age and said which of them would die first, which second, and which next in order after that. But he holds that men dream through the impulse of the gods in three ways: in one, because the soul foresees by itself, since it is bound by kinship with the gods;

passages.original: quorum alia sunt posita in monumentis et disciplina, quod Etruscorum declarant et haruspicini et fulgurales et tonitruales libri, vestri etiam augurales; alia autem subito ex tempore coniectura explicantur, ut apud Homerum Calchas, qui ex passerum numero belli Troiani annos auguratus est; et ut in Sullae scriptum historia videmus, quod te inspectante factum est, ut, cum ille in agro Nolano immolaret ante praetorium, ab infima ara subito anguis emergeret, cum quidem C.
passages.english: Of these, some are set down in records and in a body of teaching, as is shown by the Etruscan books on haruspicy, on lightning, and on thunder, and also by your augural books; others are interpreted on the spur of the moment by conjecture, like Calchas in Homer, who foretold from the number of the sparrows the years of the Trojan War; and as we see written in Sulla's history, of a thing that happened while you watched: when he was sacrificing before his headquarters in the territory of Nola, a snake suddenly emerged from the base of the altar, whereupon Gaius
passages.notes: The sentence breaks off at 'C.' (Gaius), continuing into the following context with 'Postumius the haruspex'.

passages.original: Atque etiam illa concitatio declarat vim in animis esse divinam. negat enim sine furore Democritus quemquam poëtam magnum esse posse, quod idem dicit Plato. quem, si placet, appellet furorem, dum modo is furor ita laudetur, ut in Phaedro Platonis laudatus est. quid? vestra oratio in causis, quid ipsa actio potest esse vehemens et gravis et copiosa, nisi est animus ipse commotior?
passages.english: And that excitement too shows that there is a divine power in souls. For Democritus denies that anyone can be a great poet without madness, and Plato says the same. Let him call it madness, if he likes, provided that this madness is praised as it is praised in Plato's Phaedrus. What of your own speaking in lawsuits? How can the delivery itself be vehement, weighty and abundant unless the mind itself is more than usually stirred?
passages.notes: The subject of 'appellet' (let him call) is unclear; probably Plato, or 'anyone'.

passages.original: Quis est autem quem non moveat clarissimis monumentis testata consignataque antiquitas? Calchantem augurem scribit Homerus longe optimum, eumque ducem classium fuisse ad Ilium, auspiciorum credo scientia, non locorum.
passages.english: And who is there who is not moved by antiquity attested and sealed by the most illustrious records? Homer writes that Calchas was by far the best augur, and that he was the leader of the fleets to Ilium—by his knowledge of auspices, I suppose, not of the regions.

passages.original: amphilochus et Mopsus Argivorum reges fuerunt, sed eidem augures, eique urbis in ora maritima Ciliciae Graecas condiderunt; atque etiam ante hos Amphiaraus et Tiresias non humiles et obscuri neque eorum similes, ut apud Ennium est, quí sui quaestus caúsa fictas súscitant senténtias. sed clari et praestantes viri, qui avibus et signis admoniti futura dicebant; quorum de altero etiam apud inferos Homerus ait 'solum sapere, ceteros umbrarum vagari modo'; Amphiaraum autem sic honoravit fama Graeciae, deus ut haberetur, atque ut ab eius solo, in quo est humatus, oracla peterentur.
passages.english:
Amphilochus and Mopsus were kings of the Argives, but also augurs, and they founded Greek cities on the coast of Cilicia; and even before them Amphiaraus and Tiresias were not lowly and obscure men, nor like those, as it is in Ennius,
who for the sake of their own gain stir up invented pronouncements,
but famous and outstanding men, who, warned by birds and signs, foretold the future. Of one of them Homer says that even in the underworld "he alone is wise, the rest wander like shades"; Amphiaraus, moreover, the renown of Greece so honoured that he was held to be a god, and oracles were sought from the ground where he was buried.

passages.original: Atque ille Romuli auguratus pastoralis, non urbanus fuit, nec fictus ad opiniones inperitorum, sed a certis acceptus et posteris traditus. itaque Romulus augur, ut apud Ennium est, cum fratre item augure curantes magna cum cura tum concupientes regni dant operam simul auspicio augurioque.hinc Remus auspicio se devovet atque secundam solus avem servat. at Romulus pulcher in alto quaerit Aventino, servat genus altivolantum.certabant, urbem Romam Remoramne vocarent.omnibus cura viris, uter esset induperator.exspectant;
passages.english:
And that augury of Romulus was pastoral, not urban, nor invented to suit the opinions of the ignorant, but received from reliable [men] and handed down to posterity. So Romulus the augur, as it is in Ennius, with his brother, likewise an augur:
Then, taking great care and both desiring the kingship,
they devote themselves at once to auspice and augury.
Here Remus gives himself to the auspice and alone
watches for a favourable bird. But handsome Romulus on the high
Aventine seeks, watches for the high-flying race.
They were contending whether to call the city Roma or Remora.
All the men were anxious which would be ruler.
They wait;

passages.original: Eiusdem generis etiam illud est, quod scribit Herodotus, Croesi filium, cum esset infans, locutum; quo ostento regnum patris et domum funditus concidisse. caput arsisse Servio Tullio dormienti quae historia non prodidit? ut igitur, qui se tradit quieti praeparato animo cum bonis cogitationibus, tum rebus ad tranquillitatem accommodatis, certa et vera cernit in somnis;
passages.english: Of the same kind too is what Herodotus writes: that Croesus' son spoke when he was an infant, and that by this portent his father's kingdom and house utterly collapsed. What history has not recorded that Servius Tullius' head blazed while he slept? So, just as one who gives himself up to rest with a mind prepared both by good thoughts and by circumstances suited to tranquillity sees certain and true things in his dreams,

passages.original: Scriptum est item, cum Critonis, sui familiaris, oculum alligatum vidisset, quaesivisse, quid esset; cum autem ille respondisset in agro, ambulanti ramulum adductum, ut remissus esset, in oculum suum recidisse, tum Socrates: 'Non enim paruisti mihi revocanti, cum uterer, qua soleo, praesagitione divina.' Idem etiam Socrates, cum apud Delium male pugnatum esset Lachete praetore fugeretque cum ipso Lachete, ut ventum est in trivium, eadem, qua ceteri, fugere noluit.
passages.english: It is written likewise that when [Socrates] saw the eye of Crito, his friend, bandaged, he asked what it was; and when Crito answered that as he was walking in the country a branch, pulled back, had sprung back into his eye when it was let go, then Socrates [said]: "Because you did not obey me when I called you back, using, as I usually do, divine foreknowledge." The same Socrates, too, when the battle at Delium had gone badly under the command of Laches and he was fleeing with Laches himself, when they came to a crossroads, refused to flee by the same road as the rest.

passages.original: Quocirca primum mihi videtur, ut Posidonius facit, a deo, de quo satis dictum est, deinde a fato, deinde a natura, vis omnis divinandi ratioque repetenda. fieri igitur omnia fato ratio cogit fateri. fatum autem id appello, quod Graeci edJuap/evrv, id est ordinem seriemque causarum, cum causae causa nexa rem ex se gignat.
passages.english: Therefore it seems to me that, as Posidonius does, the whole power and principle of divination must be traced first from god, of whom enough has been said, then from fate, then from nature. Reason, then, compels us to admit that all things happen by fate. And I call fate what the Greeks call *heimarmenē*, that is, an order and series of causes, when cause linked to cause produces a thing out of itself.
passages.notes: The Greek word εἱμαρμένη is garbled in the scan ("edJuap/evrv").

passages.original: Democritus autem censet sapienter instituisse veteres, ut hostiarum immolatarum inspicerentur exta; quorum ex habitu atque ex colore tum salubritatis, tum pestilentiae signa percipi, non numquam etiam, quae sit vel sterilitas agrorum vel fertilitas futura.
passages.english: Democritus, moreover, holds that the ancients wisely established that the entrails of sacrificed victims should be inspected, since from their condition and colour signs are perceived now of healthiness, now of pestilence, and sometimes even of what the barrenness or fertility of the fields will be.

passages.original: Addunt ad extremum, 'omnia levius casura rebus divinis procuratis.' Si autem nihil fit extra fatum, nihil levari re divina potest. hoc sentit Homerus cum querentem Iovem inducit quod Sarpedonem filium a morte contra fatum eripere non posset. hoc idem significat Graecus ille in eam sententiam versus: quod fóre paratum est, ìd summum exsuperát Iovem.totum omnino fatum etiam Atellanio versu iure mihi esse irrisum videtur;
passages.english: They add at the end: 'everything will fall out more lightly if the rites have been performed to avert it.' But if nothing happens outside fate, nothing can be lightened by a rite. Homer has this in mind when he brings in Jupiter complaining that he could not snatch his son Sarpedon from death against fate. The same thing is expressed by that Greek verse to this effect: 'What is ready to be, that overpowers highest Jupiter.' The whole idea of fate seems to me to have been rightly mocked even in a line of an Atellan farce;

passages.original: sed tamen eo concesso qui evenit, ut is, qui impetrire velit, convenientem hostiam rebus suis immolet? hoc erat, quod ego non rebar posse dissolvi. At quam festive dissolvitur! pudet me non tui quidem, cuius etiam memoriam admiror, sed Chrysippi, Antipatri, Posidonii, qui idem istuc quidem dicunt, quod est dictum a te, ad hostiam deligendam ducem esse vim quandam sentientem atque divinam, quae toto confusa mundo sit.
passages.english: But even granting that, how does it come about that the man who wishes to obtain favourable omens sacrifices a victim suited to his affairs? This was what I thought could not be resolved. But how neatly it is resolved! I am ashamed, not of you indeed, whose memory I even admire, but of Chrysippus, Antipater, and Posidonius, who say exactly what you have said: that in choosing the victim the guide is a certain sentient and divine power diffused through the whole world.
passages.notes: "impetrire" read as the augural verb impetrire (to obtain favourable omens).

passages.original: Democritus quidem optimis verbis causam explicat cur ante lucem galli canant; depulso enim de pectore et in omne corpus diviso et mitificato cibo cantus edere quiete satiatos; qui quidem ' silentio noctis,' ut ait Ennius, favent faucíbus russis cantu plausuque prem'int alas.cum igitur hoc animal tam sit canorum sua sponte, quid in mentem venit Callistheni dicere deos gallis signum dedisse cantandi, cum id vel natura vel casus efficere potuisset?
passages.english: Democritus, indeed, explains in excellent words the reason why cocks crow before daylight: for when the food has been driven down from the breast and distributed through the whole body and softened, they utter their songs, sated with rest; and they, "in the silence of the night," as Ennius says, "indulge their ruddy throats in song and beat their wings." Since, then, this creature is so given to song of its own accord, what came into Callisthenes' mind to say that the gods had given the cocks a sign to crow, when either nature or chance could have brought this about?
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'faucíbus' for 'faucibus', 'prem'int' for 'premunt'. The Ennius quotation is verse.

passages.original: Nam illud mirarer—si crederem—quod apud Homerum Calchantem dixisti ex passerum numero belli Troiani annos auguratum; de cuius coniectura sic apud Homerum, ut nos otiosi convertimus, loquitur Agamemnon: ferte, viri, et duros animo tolerate labores,auguris ut nostri Calchantis fata queamus scire ratosne habeant an vanos pectoris orsus.namque omnes memori portentum mente retentant,qui non funestis liquerunt lumina fatis.argolicis primum ut vestita est classibus Aulis,quae Priamo cladem et Troiae pestemque ferebant, nos circum latices gelidos fumantibus aris,aurigeris divom placantes numina tauris,sub platano umbrifera, fons unde emanat aquai,vidimus immani specie tortuque draconem terribilem, Iovis ut pulsu penetrabat ab ara;qui platani in ramo foliorum tegmine saeptos corripuit pullos;
passages.english:
For I would wonder at that, if I believed it, which you mentioned from Homer: that Calchas foretold the years of the Trojan War from the number of sparrows. Of his interpretation Agamemnon speaks thus in Homer, as I translated it in my leisure: "Bear up, men, and endure hard labours with your spirit,
so that we may know whether the prophecies of our augur Calchas
hold valid or empty the utterances of his breast.
For all retain the portent in mindful memory
who have not left the light by deadly fates.
When first Aulis was clothed with the Argive fleets,
which were bearing ruin to Priam and destruction to Troy,
we, around the cool waters, at the smoking altars,
appeasing the powers of the gods with gold-horned bulls,
beneath a shady plane tree, from where a spring of water flows,
saw a serpent of monstrous aspect and coils,
terrible, as it came forth from the altar at the impulse of Jupiter;
it seized the nestlings hidden by a covering of leaves
on a branch of the plane tree;
passages.notes: Verse lines run together in the source; lineation restored. 'aquai' is archaic genitive of 'aqua'.

passages.original: quae autem est inter augures conveniens et coniuncta constantia? ad nostri auguri consuetudinem dixit Ennius: tum tonuit laevum bene tempestate serena.
passages.english: And what consistent and coherent agreement is there among the augurs? Following the practice of our augury Ennius said: "Then it thundered on the left, auspiciously, in clear weather."
passages.notes: 'laevum bene' may be taken as 'favourably on the left'; left-hand thunder was a favourable sign in Roman augury.

passages.original: illudne dubium est, quin multi, cum ita nati essent, ut quaedam contra naturam depravata haberent, restituerentur et corrigerentur ab natura, cum se ipsa revocasset, aut arte atque medicina? ut, quorum linguae sic inhaererent, ut loqui non possent, eae scalpello resectae liberarentur. multi etiam naturae vitium meditatione atque exercitatione sustulerunt, ut Demosthenem scribit Phalereus, cum rho dicere nequiret, exercitatione fecisse, ut planissime diceret. quodsi haec astro ingenerata et tradita essent, nulla res ea mutare posset. quid? dissimilitudo locorum nonne dissimilis hominum procreationes habet?
passages.english: Is there any doubt that many, when they had been born so as to have certain parts deformed contrary to nature, were restored and corrected by nature, when she had recovered herself, or by art and medicine? For example, those whose tongues were so tied that they could not speak were freed by having them cut loose with a scalpel. Many too have removed a natural defect by practice and exercise, as Phalereus writes that Demosthenes, when he could not say rho, by exercise brought it about that he pronounced it very clearly. But if these things had been implanted and handed down by a star, nothing could change them. What then? Does not difference of places produce different kinds of human offspring?

passages.original: quis enim est qui credat Apollinis ex oraculo Pyrrho esse responsum: aio te, Aeacida, Romanos vincere posse?primum Latine Apollo numquam locutus est; deinde ista sors inaudita Graecis est; praeterea Pyrrhi temporibus iam Apollo versus facere desierat; postremo, quamquam semper fuit, ut apud Ennium est, stolidum genus Aeacidarum,bellipotentes sunt magis quam sapientipotentes, tamen hanc amphiboliam versus intellegere potuisset, 'vincere te Romanos' nihilo magis in se quam in Romanos valere;
passages.english: For who is there who would believe that Pyrrhus received this reply from the oracle of Apollo: "I say that you, descendant of Aeacus, the Romans can conquer"? First, Apollo never spoke in Latin; next, that oracle is unknown to the Greeks; besides, in Pyrrhus' time Apollo had already stopped composing verses; finally, although, as Ennius has it, "the race of the Aeacidae was always dull-witted," "mighty in war rather than mighty in wisdom," yet he could have understood the ambiguity of this line, that "you the Romans to conquer" applied no more against himself than against the Romans;
passages.notes: The oracle's Latin 'aio te, Aeacida, Romanos vincere posse' is ambiguous: either 'you can conquer the Romans' or 'the Romans can conquer you'; the English keeps the ambiguous order. 'bellipotentes ... sapientipotentes' are Ennian coinages.

passages.original: Utrum igitur censemus dormientium animos per sene ipsos in somniando moveri, an, ut Democritus censet, externa et adventicia visione pulsari? sive enim sic est sive illo modo, videri possunt permulta somniantibus falsa pro veris. nam et navigantibus moveri videntur ea quae stant, et quodam obtutu oculorum duo pro uno lucernae lumina.
passages.english: Do we think, then, that the minds of sleepers are moved of themselves in dreaming, or, as Democritus thinks, are struck by an external and incoming vision? For whether it is this way or that, a great many false things can seem true to dreamers. For to people sailing, things that stand still seem to move, and with a certain fixing of the eyes two lamp-flames appear instead of one.
passages.notes: 'per sene ipsos' is evidently a scanning error for 'per se ipsos'.

passages.original: Iam vero quis dicere audeat vera omnia esse somnia? 'Aliquot somnia vera,' inquit Ennius, 'sed omnia non est necesse.' Quae est tandem ista distinctio? quae vera, quae falsa habet? et, si vera a deo mittuntur, falsa unde nascuntur? nam si ea quoque divina quid inconstantius deo? quid inscitius autem est quam mentes mortalium falsis et mendacibus visis concitare?
passages.english: Now, who would dare to say that all dreams are true? "Some dreams are true," says Ennius, "but it is not necessary that all are." What, pray, is that distinction? What does it count as true, what as false? And if the true ones are sent by god, where do the false ones arise from? For if these too are divine, what is more inconstant than god? And what is more foolish than to stir up the minds of mortals with false and lying visions?

passages.original: naturam autem eam dico, qua numquam animus insistens agitatione et motu esse vacuus potest. is cum languore corporis nec membris uti nec sensibus potest, incidit in visa varia et incerta ' ex reliquiis,' ut ait Aristoteles, 'inhaerentibus earum rerum, quas vigilans gesserit aut cogitaverit.' Quarum perturbatione mirabiles interdum existunt species somniorum; quae si alia falsa, alia vera, qua nota internoscantur, scire sane velim.
passages.english: And I call that its nature by which the mind can never be at rest and free of agitation and motion. When, through the languor of the body, it can use neither limbs nor senses, it falls into varied and uncertain visions 'from the remnants,' as Aristotle says, 'clinging of those things which it did or thought while awake.' From the disturbance of these, marvellous kinds of dreams sometimes arise; and if some of these are false, others true, I should very much like to know by what mark they are distinguished.

passages.original: Chrysippus quidem divinationem definit his verbis: 'vim cognoscentem et videntem et explicantem signa, quae a dis hominibus portendantur; officium autem esse eius praenoscere, dei erga homines mente qua sint quidque significent, quem ad modumque ea procurentur atque expientur.' Idemque somniorum coniectionem definit hoc modo: 'esse vim cernentem et explanantem, quae a dis hominibus significentur in somnis.' Quid ergo? ad haec mediocri opus est prudentia an et ingenio praestanti et eruditione perfecta?
passages.english: Chrysippus indeed defines divination in these words: 'a power that recognises, sees and explains the signs which are portended by the gods to men; and its function is to know beforehand in what disposition the gods are towards men and what they signify, and how these things may be averted and expiated.' And he likewise defines the interpretation of dreams thus: 'a power that perceives and explains what is signified by the gods to men in dreams.' What then? Is there need for ordinary good sense for these things, or for outstanding talent and perfect learning?

passages.original: quam multi inopes digni praesidio deorum nullo somnio ad thesaurum reperiendum admonentur! quam autem ob causam tam est obscure admonitus ut ex ovo nasceretur thesauri similitudo, potius quam aperte thesaurum quaerere iuberetur, sicut aperte Simonides vetitus est navigare?
passages.english: How many poor people, worthy of the gods' protection, are prompted by no dream to find a treasure! And for what reason was he prompted so obscurely, so that a likeness to a treasure arose from an egg, rather than being openly told to look for treasure, just as Simonides was openly forbidden to sail?

passages.original: quem enim tu Marium visum a me putas? 'Speciem,' credo, eius et 'imaginem,' ut Democrito videtur. unde profectam 'imaginem'? 'A corporibus' enim solidis et a certis figuris vult fluere 'imagines.' Quod igitur Marii corpus erat? 'Ex eo,' inquit, 'quod fuerat.' Ista igitur me 'imago' Mari in campum Atinatem persequebatur?
passages.english: For what Marius do you think was seen by me? His 'likeness,' I suppose, and 'image,' as Democritus holds. From where did the 'image' set out? For he will have it that 'images' flow 'from' solid 'bodies' and from definite shapes. What body of Marius, then, was there? 'From that,' he says, 'which had been.' So that 'image' of Marius was following me onto the plain of Atina?
